title: Construction stocks: how to analyze builders and contractors
description: Construction stocks are driven by the order backlog, fixed-price risk and percentage of completion — here is how to read a contractor's economics.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Construction stocks are shares in companies that build what society rests on: roads, bridges, hospitals, offices and homes. The business has a property few other industries share — the product does not exist when the price is set. The contract is signed today for a facility to be completed in two to three years, built with materials, labor and machinery that cost whatever they cost at that moment. The facility is also a factory that is torn down when the work is done: every project starts with a new site, new subcontractors and new risk. The accounts therefore follow different rules than in most industries, and analyzing construction stocks comes down to three mechanisms: the order backlog, fixed-price risk and percentage of completion. Here is how they work — with Skanska, NCC and Veidekke as worked examples.

## Construction stocks live in the future — the order backlog is the heart

The order backlog is the contracted but not yet performed volume: signed contracts whose revenues are booked in coming years. [The construction contracting course](/kurser/se-22-byggentreprenaden) describes it as a revenue machine that ideally covers two to three years of sales. Reality varies. Skanska reported 257.9 billion kronor in order backlog at the end of 2025, against sales of 176.7 billion — that is 1.46 years of production. NCC held a backlog around 54.4 billion against sales of 55.7 billion, almost exactly one year. The order of the picture is the order of the income statement: order intake (new contracts) comes first, sales (performed work) comes after. Skanska's order intake in 2025 landed at 179.5 billion against 207.9 billion the year before, minus 13.7 percent — while Veidekke went the other way and lifted its order book from 41.0 to 47.3 billion Norwegian kronor, plus 15.4 percent. Same industry, two cycle positions: the backlog is the [business cycle indicator](/kurser/ma-04-konjunkturindikatorerna) that decides the difference between them.

## Two engines: contracting and project development

Most construction stocks carry two distinct revenue engines. Contracting is a service business: the company performs work for a client against payment, with thin margins on large volumes — the margin is bought with discipline in purchasing, planning and production, not with a brand. Project development (homes and commercial property) is instead a balance sheet business: the company buys land, obtains permits, builds and sells, with higher margins per project but with capital tied up in inventory and a cycle governed by interest rates and the housing market's temperature. The course's contrast is a civil engineering company with multi-year infrastructure orders against a housing developer in the interest rate cycle — the same industry label, two entirely different risk profiles. When you analyze a construction stock, the first step is therefore to sort revenue and earnings across the two engines; consolidated figures hide that volume growth and the margin cycle often come from different places.

## Fixed price: the industry's sold inflation option

A fixed-price contract means the contractor promises today's price for tomorrow's costs — economically, the company has sold an inflation option. [The order book and pricing course](/kurser/km-069-orderbok-och-prissattning) shows the mechanism in a worked example (constructed for teaching): a contract of 1,000 with a budgeted cost of 900 carries a margin of 100, that is 10.0 percent of the contract sum. Cost inflation of 8 percent without price escalation raises the cost to 972 and squeezes the margin to 28 — 2.8 percent. At 12 percent inflation the cost becomes 1,008 and the margin minus 8, minus 0.8 percent: the deal loses money without a single mistake being made on the site. With 50 percent price escalation — the price rises by half the cost increase, to 1,036 — the margin lands at 64, or 6.4 percent. The conclusion is therefore as legal as it is economic: the clauses on indexation, risk sharing and price adjustment are the most important reading in a construction stock's contracts and annual report.

## Percentage of completion — earnings and cash are two curves

Revenue in a construction project is not booked when the invoice is sent, but when the work is performed. The accounting standard IFRS 15 lets companies building facilities over time earn revenue by degree of completion — percentage of complete. The course's bridge example: a contract of 800 with the first year's degree of completion at 60 percent gives revenue of 480 (0.60 × 800) and earnings of 36 — 7.5 percent of revenue. But cash can at the same time be plus 60, thanks to advance payments from the client. Earnings and cash are thus two curves that meet only at final settlement, and the balance sheet carries the difference: work in progress, advances from clients and retention are the three items [the liquidity course](/kurser/v11-likviditet) teaches you to read. A construction stock can show strong earnings while cash drains — and the other way around; that is why [the quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten) should always be read in two columns, income statement and cash flow statement side by side. The distance between the curves is also the reason contracting groups report cash flow separately from earnings: that is where the mechanics of percentage of completion shows most clearly.

## How to read a construction company's accounts

Thin margins on large volumes are the industry's economics. Skanska's sales grew from 163,174 to 176,658 million kronor between 2022 and 2025 — plus 8.3 percent — while earnings fell from 8,256 to 5,702 million, minus 30.9 percent. Revenue thus grows into production without the surplus following: the 2025 net margin became 3.2 percent (5,702/176,658). The universe's TTM picture (raw data 2026-09-15) gives Skanska an operating margin of 3.9 percent, gross margin 8.9 percent, ROE 11.1 percent, ROIC 9.1 percent and debt per equity of 0.25 — a balance sheet that withstands cycles, with a margin that does not forgive mistakes. For NCC, 2025 sales became 55.7 billion (minus 9.6 percent against 61.6 billion) with an operating result of 1,938 million — 3.5 percent. Veidekke reported a full-year margin of 4.8 percent. The margin per business area says more than consolidated figures: the contracting business carries the volume, housing development carries the margin — and the cycle risk.

## Valuation: thin margins against a secured backlog

In the universe's measurement Skanska carried the valuation P/E 16.4, EV/EBIT 13.8, P/B 1.76 and a free cash flow yield of 7.8 percent of the market value, with forecast growth of plus 10.9 percent. Multiple comparisons between construction stocks should still be read with care. Because earnings are a derivative of fixed-price outcomes and cycle position, a low [P/E ratio](/kurser/km-009-pe) can be a peak-cycle phenomenon — earnings look cheap exactly when they are at their best. [EV/EBIT](/kurser/km-010-evebit) against the backlog's coverage time says more: a backlog above one year at a company with escalation clauses carries a different risk than the same multiple without them. The housing development arm also follows [the housing market's mechanics](/kurser/ma-08-bostadsmarknadens-mekanik) — the interest rate governs housing starts, housing starts govern order intake, and order intake governs sales with a delay of a couple of years.

## Checklist: six questions when you analyze a construction stock

1. **Backlog coverage** — how many years of sales are contracted?
2. **Order intake against sales** — is the revenue machine growing or shrinking?
3. **Price escalation clauses** — who carries the inflation in fixed-price contracts?
4. **Work in progress against advances** — do cash or earnings carry the facility?
5. **Margin per business area** — how much of the result is project development?
6. **Cycle position** — where in the rate and housing cycle does order intake stand?

The method is the same as in [the sector analysis's three questions](/kurser/se-16-sektoranalysens-metod): the revenue engine, the margin engine and the balance between them.

Construction stocks reward those who read forward. The order backlog is contracted future, the fixed price is a sold inflation option, and percentage of completion makes earnings and cash two separate curves. The three mechanisms explain why Skanska can grow sales 8.3 percent while earnings fall 30.9 percent — and why the order book says more about tomorrow than last year's annual report. The industries' median profiles are in [the industry medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2), and the complete method in [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026).

_Sources: [Skanska](https://group.skanska.com/investors/) year-end report 2025; [NCC](https://www.ncc.com) interim report and annual report 2025; [Veidekke](https://www.veidekke.com/investor-relations/) Q4 2025; AK1A's 100-company universe (StockAnalysis/S&P Global, raw data 2026-09-15); worked examples constructed for teaching from the [Construction Contracting](/kurser/se-22-byggentreprenaden) course._

_This is educational financial analysis, not investment advice._
